preserved_peer_crosscheck.assessment: SPOT 4. OL's challenge is sound and I support it. Verified oshb Lev.12.7: וְהִקְרִיבוֹ לִפְנֵי יְהוָה וְכִפֶּר עָלֶיהָ וְטָהֲרָה מִמְּקֹר דָּמֶיהָ זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה -- the colophon explicitly reads 'this is the law of her who bears, whether for a male or for a female,' which by its own wording brackets BOTH the timeline material (12:2-5, differentiated by sex) AND the offering procedure (12:6-7) as one torah. The internal seam the draft relies on to split at 12:5/12:6 is a temporal-transition clause (ובמלאת ימי טהרה, 'when the days of her purification are completed'), not a fresh casuistic protasis (אם/כי) of the kind that elsewhere drives the draft's splits, and no MT paragraph marker corroborates it -- oshb ch.12 supplies no visible internal structural break, consistent with OL's claim that the chapter's material runs as one unit through v.8. I weighed the strongest counter-argument (the draft's own precedent at 7:11-36, where a single zot torat superscription governing all peace-offering material is nonetheless split into five separate decisions based on internal occasion-changes) and find it distinguishable: at 7:11ff the superscription sits at the START and is followed by MULTIPLE fresh protases marking genuinely distinct occasions/topics (thanksgiving v.12, vow/freewill v.16, purity-contact v.19, fat/blood v.22, priestly portions v.28) -- exactly the kind of repeated tier-1 signal that justifies fragmentation. Ch.12 by contrast has only ONE internal transition (description-to-procedure) within a single, tightly-unified case (childbirth purification for one woman), and its colophon sits at the END, explicitly closing what it names as one torah -- functionally closer to how the draft treats 7:37-38 and 11:46-47 (both self-contained, non-fragmented closing summaries) than to 7:11's opening superscription. The challenge correctly identifies that the text's own bracketing language was under-weighted relative to a comparatively weak internal transition marker.

preserved_primary_reviews.rationale: The decision's own rationale identifies v.11 as a 'resumptive repetition' of v.6 ('Aaron shall present the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself' is repeated almost verbatim). That observation is textually accurate, but I think it argues for the opposite conclusion from the one drawn. Resumptive repetition (Wiederaufnahme) is a recognized device for bracketing an inserted unit within a single continuing action, not for marking two independent actions -- v.6 only announces the bull-offering as a headline ('Aaron shall offer the bull...and make atonement'), the goat-lot casting (7-10) is a necessary but structurally embedded digression (the lots must be cast before v.15 can refer to 'the goat of the sin offering for the people'), and v.11-14 is where the bull action v.6 announced is actually completed (kill, take blood, take coals, sprinkle). Splitting at v.10/11 cuts through the middle of what the text itself marks, via the repetition, as one interrupted-and-resumed action for Aaron's own atonement, rather than at a point where a genuinely new independent action begins. Under the campaign's own larger-unit preference, and given there is no fresh protasis, addressee, or register change anywhere in 6-14 (all third-person sequential deontic 'shall' clauses about Aaron), I think 16:6-14 reads better as one unit: Aaron's complete sin-offering procedure for himself, including the goat-lot digression it depends on.

preserved_author_responses.response: Accepted. 16:11's near-verbatim repetition of 16:6 is classic Wiederaufnahme: a proleptic summary (v.6), a structurally necessary digression (the goat-lot casting of vv.7-10, needed before v.15 can name 'the goat for the people'), and a resumption that continues the interrupted action through v.14, not a second independent opening. The real, stronger seam is v.15's new sacrificial object and widening scope, on which M8-Lev-095 already rests. Merging 16:6-10 and 16:11-14 into one span.
